subject: history_social
passage: In England before the nineteenth century, few villages had accurate maps, and the boundaries of a parish, the district served by a local church, were often marked by nothing more than a stream, a hedge, or a large stone. Once a year, in a custom called "beating the bounds," the people of a parish walked the entire boundary together. Children were brought along and, at each boundary marker, were gently bumped against the stone or made to recite where the line ran. The involvement of children suggests that one purpose of the custom was to ______
stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: teach children the religious duties they would take on as adults.
choices.B: replace the old stone markers with written records of the boundary.
choices.C: pass knowledge of the boundary on to a new generation so it would not be forgotten.
choices.D: allow the parish to extend its boundary a little further each year.

explanation.why: Without maps, the boundary existed mainly in people's memories. Bringing children to each marker and making them remember it would ensure that, when the adults were gone, someone would still know where the line ran.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text describes learning the location of a boundary, not religious duties.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The custom relied on memory and physical markers; the text mentions no written records being made.
explanation.C: Correct. Making children memorize the markers preserves boundary knowledge across generations in the absence of maps.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The walk followed the existing boundary; nothing suggests the line was moved.
